sections.title: The RIP-2 Documents
sections.content:
As required by RFC 1264, this report documents RIP-2's main features and implementation experience. It is informational and does not itself specify an Internet standard.

The applicability statement is in RFC 1722, the protocol description in RFC 1723, and the MIB description in RFC 1724. This memo obsoletes RFC 1387.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a report about RIP-2, not the protocol specification itself. It points readers to separate documents for the rules and management information.

sections.title: Features Added to RIP-1
sections.content:
RIP-2 shares the basic algorithms of RIP-1 and adds external route tags, subnet masks, next hop addresses and authentication. It also allows packets to be multicast instead of broadcast. The domain field from the earlier version was removed and left reserved because there was no clear agreement on its use.

Route tags can carry information obtained from an exterior gateway protocol, such as an autonomous system number. Subnet masks support variable subnet masks and classless addressing. A next hop address can identify a better next router. The authentication mechanism is extensible, but the memo defines only a plain-text password.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP-2 adds fields for route information, subnet sizes and a better next router. It also adds authentication and can send updates to a multicast address.

sections.title: The RIP-2 Management Information Base
sections.content:
The RIP-2 MIB lets operators monitor and control RIP inside a router. It includes global and per-interface counters and controls, as well as per-peer counters that show the status of RIP-2 neighbors.

The MIB was changed to remove the domain field and converted to version 2 format.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB contains counters and controls for RIP, its interfaces and its neighbors. It gives an operator information about the protocol inside a router.

sections.title: Implementations and Experience
sections.content:
The memo names three complete implementations: GATED, Xylogics's Annex Communication server and an implementation for NOS. The author tested GATED with the Xylogics implementation and found no incompatibilities, including in the authentication mechanism.

Xylogics had run RIP-2 on production systems for five months. The only reported problem was that some routers discarded version 2 packets instead of ignoring fields not defined for version 1, contrary to RFC 1058.
sections.plainLanguage: The author reports three complete implementations and a successful interoperability test between two of them. Some routers did not handle new-version packets as expected.
